sentences.text: A nearly complete fossil was recovered, though the front limbs were absent after falling into a sinkhole prior to excavation.
Research shows that young individuals possessed a frill that was narrower at the rear and proportionally shorter than those of adults.
Lawrence Morris Lambe first identified Chasmosaurus remains in 1898, although the initial name Protorosaurus was already in use for another creature.
Every specimen of this dinosaur has been unearthed within the Dinosaur Park Formation in Alberta, Canada.
As a quadrupedal herbivore, Chasmosaurus likely maintained a more selective diet than other ceratopsians because of its elongated snout and jaw structure.
Fossil evidence from Alberta suggests these animals lived in groups, and mass death sites indicate a rapid demise caused by a catastrophic event such as a volcanic eruption.
Some studies propose that a herd perished while trying to cross a flooded river, a theory supported by matrix evidence suggesting a juvenile drowned during such an attempt.
Scientists hypothesize that males might have formed a defensive circle with their frills facing outward to protect against predators like Daspletosaurus.
A juvenile specimen found in Alberta, measuring about 1.8 meters in length and estimated to be three years old, implies the species may have cared for its young.
Evidence indicates the dinosaur was not a fast mover, meaning young ones did not need to run quickly to match the speed of adults.
Chasmosaurus belli is the type species of the genus, while Chasmosaurus russelli was described by Charles Mortram Sternberg in 1940 based on specimen NMC 8800.
In 1915, Lambe placed Chasmosaurus within the subfamily Chasmosaurinae under the broader group Ceratopsia.
A 2016 analysis proposed that the size of postorbital horns varies too much to reliably separate different species of Chasmosaurus.
Although initially treated as separate species, it is now possible that long horns belonged to males and shorter horns to females.
This ceratopsid lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, spanning from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago in North America.
Chasmosaurus shared its environment on the eastern coast of Laramidia with successive species of Centrosaurus.
Researchers consider the function of the frill and horns to be a problematic issue.
Several research teams have questioned whether the genus Mojoceratops is valid following its establishment.
There is a hypothesis linking Chasmosaurus kaiseni to Chasmosaurus canadensis, though this connection remains debated.
